chief_complaint: recurrent gross blood in urine, hypertension, and bilateral massive flank cysts on ultrasound
hpi_details: A 45-year-old man with an affected first-degree relative has hypertension and ultrasound showing markedly enlarged kidneys with numerous bilateral cysts. He has intermittent visible hematuria with flank discomfort, but no fever, dysuria, clots, trauma, or reduced urine output.
ideas: thinks the hematuria may be from polycystic kidney disease
concerns: worried about serious complications and prolonged recovery
expectations: wants to understand the cause of bleeding, kidney prognosis, and safe treatment options

clinical_knowledge.topic: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) evaluation and management
core_concepts: ADPKD is an inherited disorder with progressive bilateral renal cysts, hypertension, hematuria, nephrolithiasis, cyst infection, and risk of chronic kidney disease.

Visible hematuria may follow cyst hemorrhage or stone passage, but it still requires assessment for urinary infection, obstruction, and urothelial or renal malignancy according to risk and persistence.

Assess blood pressure, serum creatinine/eGFR, electrolytes, urinalysis with microscopy and culture when infection is possible, urine protein/albumin, and imaging appropriate to hematuria and renal function.

Blood-pressure management and kidney-protective follow-up are central; tolvaptan is considered only by nephrology for selected adults at risk of rapid progression, after contraindication and liver-monitoring review.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: recurrent gross blood in urine, hypertension, and bilateral massive flank cysts on ultrasound
Family history plus numerous bilateral renal cysts and enlarged kidneys strongly support ADPKD.
Intermittent visible hematuria and flank discomfort can result from cyst hemorrhage, stones, infection, or a separate urinary-tract source.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Attributing every episode of gross hematuria to a ruptured cyst without considering stones, infection, anticoagulation, or malignancy.
Starting antibiotics for hematuria alone without symptoms and testing supporting infection.
Assuming tolvaptan is appropriate for every person with ADPKD.
dangerous_errors: Missing clot retention, anuria/oliguria, acute kidney injury, hemodynamic instability, or severe uncontrolled pain during a hematuria episode.
Delaying urgent assessment of fever or rigors with flank pain, which may represent cyst infection or pyelonephritis.
Ignoring sudden severe headache or focal neurologic symptoms that need emergency evaluation for possible intracranial hemorrhage.
management_principles: Check hemodynamic status, renal function, urinalysis, medication and anticoagulant use; tailor hematuria imaging and urology referral to findings and cancer risk.
Treat hypertension with a kidney-appropriate regimen and monitor eGFR, albuminuria, electrolytes, and cardiovascular risk with nephrology.
Use oral hydration and simple analgesia when safe for a stable suspected cyst bleed; avoid nephrotoxic NSAIDs in impaired kidney function and give return precautions.
Discuss genetic counseling and screening considerations for family members; evaluate intracranial aneurysm risk based on personal or family history and specialist guidance.
boundaries_and_exceptions: ACE inhibitor choice and dose depend on blood pressure, potassium, creatinine, and bilateral renal-artery disease risk; reassess renal function after initiation or titration.

Tolvaptan requires specialist selection, counseling about polyuria and hydration, and ongoing liver-function monitoring; it is contraindicated in pregnancy and requires contraceptive counseling for patients who could become pregnant.

source_refs.title: KDIGO 2025 Clinical Practice Guideline for ADPKD

reference_soap.subjective: 45-year-old man with an affected first-degree relative, hypertension, enlarged multicystic kidneys, intermittent gross hematuria, and flank discomfort. He denies fever, dysuria, clots, trauma, and reduced urine output.
reference_soap.objective: Obtain vitals, blood pressure, CBC, creatinine/eGFR, electrolytes, urinalysis with microscopy, urine culture when indicated, urine albumin/protein, and hematuria-directed imaging appropriate to renal function. Review anticoagulants and examine for volume status and flank tenderness.
reference_soap.assessment: ADPKD is likely. Cyst hemorrhage is possible, but visible hematuria also requires evaluation for stone disease, infection, obstruction, and malignancy based on clinical course and risk.
reference_soap.plan: Arrange nephrology follow-up for blood-pressure and kidney-function management and urology evaluation if hematuria persists, recurs, or has concerning features. Consider disease-modifying therapy only after specialist risk assessment. Send urgently for clots with retention, anuria, AKI, fever/rigors, instability, severe pain, or neurologic red flags.

learning_objectives: Recognize ADPKD and evaluate gross hematuria without prematurely attributing it to a cyst
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for recurrent gross blood in urine, hypertension, and bilateral massive flank cysts on ultrasound
Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for urology
Plan kidney-protective follow-up and appropriate emergency escalation

teaching.one_liner: An inherited disorder marked by progressive bilateral renal cyst formation, presenting with hypertension, flank pain or hematuria from cyst hemorrhage/rupture, and eventual progression toward chronic kidney disease.
differentials: Acquired cystic kidney disease from chronic renal failure
Renal cell carcinoma with cystic degeneration
red_flags: Infected renal cyst or pyelonephritis (fever, chills, flank pain)
Sudden severe headache suggestive of ruptured intracranial (berry) aneurysm

must_ask.objective: Family history of polycystic kidney disease
must_ask.say: Does anyone in your family have polycystic kidney disease, or has anyone needed dialysis or a kidney transplant?
Have you noticed blood in your urine, and did it come on suddenly with flank pain?
Have you been told you have high blood pressure, and if so, how well is it controlled?

must_ask.objective: Extrarenal manifestations - liver cysts, aneurysms, headaches
must_ask.say: Have you ever had a sudden severe headache, or been told you have cysts in your liver?

must_ask.objective: Recurrent UTIs and flank pain pattern
must_ask.say: Have you had recurrent urinary infections or chronic flank discomfort from the cysts?
